summary: Describes a mechanism for subscriber applications to request a continuous, customized stream of updates from a YANG datastore. This visibility into configuration and operational state changes allows remote mirroring and monitoring of devices.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking a device again and again whether anything changed, you ask it to tell you whenever something does, like a friend texting you scores as a game goes on.

questions: how to monitor yang datastore changes
what is a dampening period in yang push
subtitle: How a client can subscribe to a YANG datastore and have a device push updates instead of polling it.

tldr.problem: Polling a device for its configuration or state adds latency, can miss cycles when the network is stressed, gives uneven intervals, and wastes load when changes are rare.
tldr.mechanism: YANG-Push extends the subscription model of RFC 8639 so a subscriber picks a datastore, a selection filter and an update trigger, either periodic or on-change, and the publisher streams push-update and push-change-update notifications.
tldr.outcome: Subscribers get a continuous, filtered stream of datastore updates, with rules for dampening, access control and reporting incomplete updates. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8641 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8639, whose transport options it reuses.

sections.title: From Polling to Subscriptions
sections.content:
Traditional visibility into managed devices is built on polling: a client periodically requests data. The RFC lists the drawbacks. Polling adds significant latency, cycles may be missed or delayed when the network is under stress, uneven intervals make data hard to compare, and many polling cycles load the network and devices when changes are infrequent.

A better approach is for an application to receive automatic and continuous updates from a chosen part of a datastore. The service has two parts: applications subscribe to datastore updates, and the server, called the publisher, pushes and effectively streams them. The requirements are in RFC 7923. This document builds on RFC 8639 by adding YANG data model augmentations, extended RPCs and new datastore-specific update notifications. The transports defined in RFC 8639 work with it unchanged.
sections.eli5: Asking again and again, "Has anything changed yet?" is slow and tiring for everyone. It is better to say, "Please tell me when it does."

sections.title: The Subscription Model
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms. A datastore node is a node in the instantiated YANG data tree, a datastore subtree is a node plus all its descendants, and an update record represents one or more datastore node updates, possibly with the type of change and the subscription ID.

YANG-Push subscriptions are described by a YANG data model that enhances the RFC 8639 model. A subscription names a datastore, a selection filter and an update trigger. Two filter types exist, and a publisher MUST support at least one:

  • subtree, with the syntax and meaning of RFC 6241, Section 6;
  • xpath, an XPath expression that returns a node set.

Only one selection filter applies to a subscription at a time, and a request with a new filter replaces the old one. The YANG module is named ietf-yang-push and uses the prefix yp.
sections.eli5: A subscription says three things: which shelf to watch, which items on it you care about, and when you want to hear about them.

sections.title: Periodic and On-Change Updates
sections.content:
There are two kinds of update trigger. A periodic subscription is set by a period and an optional anchor-time. Update intervals fall on points in time that are multiples of the period from the anchor time. If no anchor time is given, it MUST be set to the creation time of the initial update record.

An on-change subscription sends an update whenever a change in the subscribed data is detected. Its extra parameters are:

  • dampening-period: the interval that must pass before the next update record for the subscription. Only the value current at the end of the period is sent for each object, and an object that returned to its old value (or was created then deleted) is still reported, which signals churn.
  • change-type (excluded-change in the model): lets a subscriber leave out some kinds of change, for example sending creations and deletions but not value changes.
  • sync-on-start: whether a complete push-update of all subscribed data is sent when the subscription starts.

On-change is harder to implement than periodic, so it may not be supported for every object. A publisher MAY accept an on-change subscription and send updates only for nodes that support it, or MAY reject it. The RFC suggests discoverable on-change support, such as the YANG data model proposed in a separate document, and says implementations SHOULD provide their own solution until one is standardized.
sections.eli5: You can ask for a report at fixed times, like a clock chiming every hour. Or you can ask to be told when something changes, and add a pause so you are not buzzed a hundred times a minute.

sections.title: Update Notifications and Their Encoding
sections.content:
Two generic notifications carry update records. A push-update holds a complete, filtered update of the datastore, equivalent to what a retrieval with the same filters would return. It is used for periodic subscriptions. For on-change subscriptions it MUST be the initial update when the receiver needs synchronizing, and MAY be sent later to resync.

A push-change-update is the most common update for on-change subscriptions and holds the changes since the last notification. It is encoded as a YANG Patch record (RFC 8072) describing how to go from the earlier state to the current one. Unlike plain RFC 8072, it may cover operational data as well as configuration, and a patch whose application changes nothing is valid, because that signals churn during a dampening period.

The publisher SHOULD use the patch-id as a counter starting at 0 that rises with each push-change-update. It MUST be reset to 0 whenever a resynchronization occurs, and after passing 4294967295. This makes lost or out-of-sequence records easy to spot. Update records for one subscription MUST NOT be resequenced before transport.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the machine sends the whole page, and sometimes it sends only a list of edits. A numbered edit list lets you notice if a page went missing.

sections.title: Managing Subscriptions and Negotiation
sections.content:
The RFC 8639 RPCs are enhanced for datastore subscriptions. A subscriber uses establish-subscription and modify-subscription, and delete-subscription is unchanged. This RFC adds resync-subscription, supported only for on-change subscriptions made with establish-subscription. The publisher must accept it and quickly follow with a push-update, or return an error.

A dynamic subscription request SHOULD be declined if the publisher may be unable to meet its terms. To avoid blind guessing, the error response can carry hints in a yang-data container, such as a suggested period, acceptable dampening periods, or estimates and limits for the number of objects and kilobytes. The hints are not a guarantee that a later request will be accepted. Appendix A lists the new error identities, for example period-unsupported, update-too-big, sync-too-big, on-change-unsupported and unchanging-selection.

Subscribers need the publisher's datastore schemas, which come from the YANG library, and a yang-library-change notification tells them when it has changed.
sections.eli5: If the machine says no, it also tells you what it could do instead, like a shopkeeper saying, "I cannot deliver every minute, but I can do every ten."

sections.title: Reliability and Publisher Capacity
sections.content:
A subscription is a promise that the publisher will provide updates under the agreed terms. The RFC requires the publisher to notify receivers immediately and reliably when it cannot keep that promise, and lets it suspend the subscription. It is far better to decline a request that cannot be met than to accept it. Feasibility depends on the trigger type, the period, the amount of subscribed data and the number of other subscriptions being served.

When a publisher cannot include all the desired objects, it MUST set the incomplete-update flag on any update record known to be missing information. It MAY suspend the subscription, and it MUST suspend if it creates no update record at all. When resuming an on-change subscription, it SHOULD generate a complete patch from the previous record. If that is impossible and sync-on-start is true, it MAY send the full contents in a push-update. Otherwise the next push-change-update MUST carry incomplete-update.

A receiver seeing that flag may wait, resync, or tear down the subscription and start a new one with a smaller scope. Loss of the underlying transport connection ends a dynamic subscription or suspends a configured one, so lost notifications cannot go unnoticed.
sections.eli5: If the machine cannot keep up, it must tell you right away that your update is missing pieces. Then you decide whether to wait, ask for everything again, or ask for something smaller.

sections.title: Receiver Authorization and Security
sections.content:
A receiver MUST only be sent updates it is authorized to see. The publisher applies access control to every push-update and push-change-update and silently omits nodes the receiver may not read, using the model of RFC 8341 extended to notifications. This makes pushed data equivalent to a normal get.

If nothing remains after access control, the result depends on the type. A periodic subscription MUST still send an empty push-update so the client does not think an update was lost. An on-change subscription MUST NOT send one, so the client learns nothing about nodes it cannot read. A publisher MAY reject, terminate or suspend a subscription with the error identity unchanging-selection when selections hit missing or forbidden data, or when permissions change.

The security section notes that the module is accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF, which use SSH and TLS as mandatory-to-implement secure transports. Writable nodes such as the selection filter and the datastore choice are sensitive, since an attacker who changes them could flood a receiver or hide changes. The security considerations of RFC 8639 also apply.
sections.eli5: The machine only tells you things you are allowed to know. And if someone sneaks in and changes what you are watching, you might get flooded with news or miss important news.
